title: Selective Language Damage with Parameter-Decomposition Subcomponents
text:
1 Introduction
A model edit that changes one behaviour usually changes others too. Model-editing work evaluates locality: inputs outside an edit’s scope should keep their predictions (Yao et al. 2023, sec. 2). ROME, for example, scores an edited fact by whether the model retains facts about nearby subjects (Meng et al. 2022, sec. 3.3).
I use deliberate language damage as a controlled test of edit selectivity: each edit is calibrated to the same target-language damage on validation text, then evaluated for its effects on another language. A demanding neighbour for a language edit is a closely related language. Zeroing the parameters or neurons most important for one language also degrades its relatives: Spanish removal raises Italian and Portuguese perplexity (Zhang et al. 2024, Table 11), and deactivating French neurons also affects Spanish (Tang et al. 2024, sec. 3.3.1).
Parameter decompositions may allow narrower edits. adVersarial Parameter Decomposition (VPD)1 approximates each weight matrix of a model by a sum of rank-one subcomponents, trained so that few are needed on any input (Bushnaq et al. 2026, sec. 2). It follows earlier attribution-based and stochastic decompositions (Braun et al. 2025; Bushnaq et al. 2025). If a subcomponent is specific to one language, an edit along it, \(W \leftarrow W + \alpha A\), might change that language and spare its relatives. This study uses Goodfire’s four-layer, 67M-parameter decoder-only model decomposed in the VPD report.
This study is a small follow-up inspired by Lucius Bushnaq’s LessWrong post, “Exploration: fine-tuning with parameter decomposition”. Bushnaq trains the scalar prefactors of selected subcomponents of the same model to suppress German. One subcomponent, chosen by its interpretation label, reaches chance-level German with little English damage and spares French and Spanish, while also damaging Italian (Bushnaq 2026). His comparison uses matched training budgets and LoRA baselines, with varying achieved effects.
I extend Bushnaq’s scalar-edit comparison to three language pairs with a fixed rule for selecting one subcomponent per target from target and English text. I match target effects on validation text and add full-matrix fine-tuning and neuron baselines.
The pairs are German (de) and Dutch (nl), Spanish (es) and Portuguese (pt), and French (fr) and Italian (it). In each pair the related language is protected: it is evaluated after selection and training. I calibrate each edit to raise target cross-entropy (CE) by τ = 0.5 or 1 nat/token on validation text.
The outcome is the CE rise of the protected language on European Parliament session text (Koehn 2005). After fixing the six edits and comparators, I evaluate them once on 58 new session dates to test whether the difference in related-language damage carries over to new text.

title: Selective Language Damage with Parameter-Decomposition Subcomponents
text:
2 Setup
The method details give window and set sizes, grids, tolerances and training recipes.
Model and subcomponents. The base model \(W_0\) is the four-layer, 67M-parameter decoder-only model decomposed in the VPD report. It was trained on a subset of the Pile (Bushnaq et al. 2026, sec. 3.1; Gao et al. 2020). Edits act on its 24 weight matrices: in each layer, the query, key, value and output projections of attention and the two MLP matrices. The decomposition supplies 38,912 rank-one subcomponents in all, each of the form \(A_c = u_c v_c^\top\). Subcomponents are named by layer, matrix and index: 0.attn.o:268 is subcomponent 268 of the attention output projection of layer 0.
The edit. An edit along subcomponent \(c\) of matrix \(m\) is \(W_m \leftarrow W_m + \alpha A_c\), with the subcomponent not normalized. In VPD every subcomponent carries a mask coefficient that equals 1 in the unedited model. The edit moves it to \(1 + \alpha\). We write \(\alpha = s \cdot a\), with a sign \(s = \pm 1\) and a dose \(a > 0\). With \(s = -1\), as for every subcomponent selected here, the coefficient is \(1 - a\): a dose below 1 shrinks the subcomponent’s contribution, a dose of 1 removes it, and a dose above 1 reverses its sign. The edit norm is \(|\alpha|\,\lVert A_c\rVert_F\).
Text and effects. Every Europarl set has one window per session date, parallel across languages. The CE rise of an edit is measured in nat/token. For each window, I subtract the base model \(W_0\)’s mean next-token CE from the edited model’s, then average these differences over windows. Each target has three overlapping draws of its Europarl training windows. The English retain pool mixes Europarl English training text, WikiText-2 validation text (Merity et al. 2017) and English-filtered Pile validation text.

2.1 Selecting the subcomponent
The rule scores each subcomponent by its local effect on target CE relative to its local effect on English output. Let \(g_c\) be the derivative of the mean target CE on the draw with respect to the subcomponent’s mask coefficient. Let \(q_c\) be the curvature of the English output along the same coordinate, estimated on the retain pool with labels sampled from \(W_0\). This estimates the directional Fisher information of the model’s predictive distribution. The rule ranks subcomponents by the gradient-to-retain-curvature score \[\frac{g_c^2}{q_c + \varepsilon \lVert A_c\rVert^2},\] where a small floor \(\varepsilon\) keeps subcomponents with almost no measured curvature from dominating.
The rule then tests a shortlist of the best-ranked subcomponents on the target training draw. For each subcomponent, with sign \(s = \operatorname{sign}(g_c)\), it raises the dose step by step up to 2. It accepts the first subcomponent whose target CE rise reaches 1 nat/token. If none does, it accepts the first that reached 0.5, and otherwise it finds no feasible subcomponent.
The rule chose the same subcomponent in all three draws of each target: 0.attn.o:268 for German, 0.attn.o:676 for Spanish and 0.attn.o:640 for French. They all lie in the attention output projection of the first layer and have sign \(-1\).


2.2 Comparators
Like the selection rule, the comparators use only target and English text for selection and training.

Rank-one LoRA (Hu et al. 2022) learns both vectors of an update to the matrix that holds the selected subcomponent, the attention output projection of layer 0. It uses the same matrix and rank as the subcomponent edit.
Full-matrix fine-tuning updates all 24 weight matrices.
Neuron edits use the top \(k\) MLP neurons ranked by how much more often they are active on the target draw than on the English retain pool. The edit scales their output weights down, with \(k\) and the scale calibrated to τ, in the spirit of language-specific neurons (Tang et al. 2024; Kojima et al. 2024).
The randomized-dictionary control applies the same selection rule to a randomized dictionary. In each matrix, one random signed permutation transforms the output coordinates of every subcomponent, and another transforms the input coordinates. This preserves their norms and pairwise angles but removes their alignment with \(W_0\).

The two learned updates are trained, one per draw, on a target CE objective plus the KL divergence from \(W_0\) on the English retain pool, for a fixed 200 steps. The final update is scaled down to reach τ.
A separate comparison family uses single subcomponents chosen by alternative selection rules:

the top subcomponent of an orthogonal matching pursuit (Pati et al. 1993; Mallat and Zhang 1993) of the full-matrix fine-tuning update or of a LoRA update trained across all matrices
a causal-importance heuristic that takes the top-1 subcomponent, adapted from Bushnaq’s top-16 procedure (Bushnaq 2026)
for German only, the previously chosen subcomponent 0.attn.o:268.

These comparisons have their own multiplicity correction and receive no confirmatory verdicts (appendix).


2.3 Calibration and the six edits
Every method is calibrated on target Europarl validation text. A short search over its dose sets the target CE rise to τ. An edit is matched if its validation effect lies within 0.02 nat/token of τ. Only matched edits enter a contrast. The effects achieved on the readout dates can differ and are reported with the results.

2.4 What was fixed, and what was known
Selection and training used only target and English text. Earlier research had used protected-language development text and identified the German subcomponent, so the selection history was not blind (Section 7.3).
I fixed the edits, comparators and analysis before evaluating them once on 58 further session dates. Those dates were not used for selection, calibration or re-matching. This tests the six fixed edits on new text in the same languages. Evaluating the selection procedure itself remains an open question.


2.5 Readouts, eligibility and intervals
Guards. English test sets determine which matched edits are usable: Europarl, WikiText-2 and Pile test text on the development readout, and English text from the confirmatory dates on the confirmatory readout. An edit is unusable if any guard’s CE rises by more than 0.1 nat/token. On the confirmatory dates it must also have been usable on development. This is an eligibility rule fixed in advance. Two usable edits can still differ greatly in how much they change English (Section 3.4).
Contrasts. For each protected-language session date, a contrast takes the CE rise of the subcomponent edit minus that of the comparator, averaged over the draws in which both are matched and usable. Its estimate is the mean over dates. Negative values mean less protected-language damage for the subcomponent edit. The claim family comprises four comparators × three pairs × two values of τ, or 24 planned contrasts.
Intervals. Every confidence interval in this paper is a simultaneous 95% interval from a bootstrap over session dates (Efron 1979), with one resample shared by every contrast of a family and the max-|t| critical value of a simultaneous band (Montiel Olea and Plagborg-Møller 2019, supplement, Algorithm 3). The intervals describe uncertainty across session dates for these fixed edits. The bootstrap varies dates while holding the draws, training seeds, subcomponents, language pairs and model fixed.
Confirmatory verdicts. Each claim contrast with a development interval receives one verdict on the confirmatory readout, according to a rule table fixed before the set was opened. It is “reproduced on confirm” if its interval excludes zero with the development sign and no used draw has a target CE rise outside τ ± 0.1. A rise outside this band is the target flag.
Post hoc analyses. Two analyses were chosen after the results were known, outside the protocol. The frozen verdicts remain those of the original analysis. The first asks whether the target effects achieved on the readout dates were comparable (Section 3.3). The second counts how often the learned updates move English less (Section 3.4).

3 Results

3.1 Target change against protected damage
All matched edits passed the English guards, and on the confirmatory dates no edit raised the target flag. Figure 1 shows each edit on the confirmatory dates as target CE rise against protected-language CE rise. At both values of τ and for all three pairs, the subcomponent edits have the lowest protected-language CE rise. Across the six subcomponent edits, the protected-language rise is 0.0003 to 0.0053 nat/token. The other methods raise it by about 0.03 to 0.88 (Table 2).






Figure 1: Target CE rise against protected CE rise for every edit on the 58 confirmatory dates (subcomponent edits: one per pair and τ, other methods: one per draw). The bands mark τ ± 0.1, the frozen tolerance of the target flag. At both values of τ the subcomponent edits raise the protected language’s CE far less than the edits calibrated to the same τ.





3.2 The protected contrasts
On the confirmatory dates, all 18 claim contrasts that have an estimate lie below zero, with upper interval ends at −0.023 or below, and every verdict is “reproduced on confirm” (Figure 2, top row, Table 4). The largest difference between a confirmatory estimate and its development estimate is 0.033.
The 18 contrasts share six subcomponent edits: each edit is compared with three comparators. The three draws vary only the comparators’ training data, so the contrasts are dependent.


3.3 Achieved target effects
The edits were calibrated to the same effect on validation text. On the readout dates the achieved effects differ somewhat (Figure 1). To assess whether less protected damage came with a smaller target effect, I estimated, post hoc, the difference in target CE rise between the subcomponent edit and each comparator, its target gap, in one simultaneous family with the protected contrasts (method details). A target gap counts as agreement if its whole interval lies within ±0.1 nat/token. This band was chosen after the results. It compares two methods and is separate from the frozen target flag, which compares one edit with τ.






Figure 2: Contrasts of the subcomponent edit with each claim comparator, on the confirmatory (filled, upper marker) and development (open, lower marker) dates, with simultaneous 95% intervals. Top: difference in protected CE rise, the frozen claim family. The axes differ between columns. Bottom: difference in achieved target CE rise, from the post hoc family of Section 3.3, with the ±0.1 nat/token agreement band. Negative values in the top row mean less protected-language damage for the subcomponent edit. Positive values in the bottom row mean a larger target effect.



On the confirmatory dates, 15 of the 18 target gaps agree by this criterion (Figure 2, bottom row). The three exceptions are all at τ = 1, and in each the point estimate lies inside the band:

German and Dutch against rank-one LoRA: +0.057 [+0.007, +0.107]
French and Italian against full-matrix fine-tuning: +0.077 [+0.020, +0.134]
French and Italian against rank-one LoRA: +0.038 [−0.027, +0.104].

On the development dates, 17 of 18 target gaps agree. The exception is French and Italian against full-matrix fine-tuning. All four exceptions have positive point estimates, though the interval for French and Italian against rank-one LoRA permits a smaller target effect for the subcomponent edit. In this larger post hoc family, all 18 protected-CE intervals and all 18 protected-KL intervals lie below zero on both readouts. Protected KL is \(D_{\mathrm{KL}}(p_{W_0} \,\|\, p_{\text{edit}})\), averaged over next-token positions on protected-language text.


3.4 English: where the learned updates are better
The guard rule only asks whether English CE rose past its limit. A finer measure is the KL divergence \(D_{\mathrm{KL}}(p_{W_0} \,\|\, p_{\text{edit}})\) of the edited model’s English next-token distribution from that of \(W_0\), averaged over positions. By this measure, both learned updates preserve English better than the subcomponent edits (Table 2). On the development readout, over three pairs × three draws × two values of τ × four English sets (the validation set and the three guards), the LoRA update has the lower KL in 72 of 72 comparisons and full-matrix fine-tuning in 65 of 72. On the English confirmatory text both have the lower KL in 18 of 18.
The subcomponent edits also change English little in absolute terms: their English KL on the confirmatory dates is below 10⁻³ nat/token. Their weight changes have larger norms: 0.29 to 0.47, against 0.12 to 0.24 for the LoRA updates and 0.07 to 0.11 for full-matrix fine-tuning. The learned updates were trained with an explicit English KL term. None of the methods had a term for the protected language. The comparison therefore measures how well the methods spare a related language absent from their training objective.

3.5 The randomized-dictionary control gave no estimate
The control applies the selection rule to the randomized dictionary. It found no feasible subcomponent in any of the 9 target–draw combinations: no shortlisted subcomponent reached even 0.5 nat/token on the target training draw within the dose limit of 2. The randomized-dictionary control therefore has no edit, and its six claim contrasts have no estimate. Because some planned contrasts are empty, the frozen analysis has the overall status “conditional” rather than “complete”.
The control was meant to measure how selective an edit of the same form is when the subcomponents are unrelated to the model’s weights. Its failure to produce an edit leaves the dictionary’s contribution unresolved. Whether a randomized subcomponent at a larger dose could spare the protected language remains unknown. The alternative subcomponent comparisons and whitened rank-one selector leave the contributions of the dictionary and selection rule unresolved as well (Section 3.6; Section 4).


3.6 Subcomponents chosen by other rules
The alternative selection comparisons use single subcomponents of the same dictionary. Every estimable contrast is at or below zero. The causal-importance heuristic picked 0.attn.o:41 in 8 of 9 target–draw combinations and, on the confirmatory dates, raised the protected CE by 0.48 to 1.37 nat/token more than the selected subcomponent, at achieved target rises close to the selected subcomponent’s (Table 5). The previously chosen German subcomponent is the selected one, so it gives an identical edit. Selectivity therefore varies among subcomponents of the same dictionary. By contrast, the randomized-dictionary control held the selection rule fixed and changed the dictionary (Section 3.5).

section: 4 Longer training and alternative rank-one directions
text:
4 Longer training and alternative rank-one directions
After the confirmatory readout, I ran exploratory comparisons on the previously evaluated development dates. The six subcomponent edits were compared with a whitened rank-one selector outside the VPD dictionary and learned updates trained for 2,000 steps, all calibrated to the same τ. All 18 protected-CE intervals of the all-run family and all 12 of the family excluding unstable learned runs lie below zero. The achieved target rises differ by at most 0.07 nat/token. The appendix gives the methods, full results and study record.
The expanded training recipe lowered the protected-language rise of full-matrix fine-tuning in all six target and τ combinations and that of LoRA in five of six. Steps, margin, grid and seeds changed together, with retention still limited to English. Convergence remains unestablished at either budget.
The whitened rank-one selector uses the selected VPD subcomponent’s norm and the main selector’s ε, leaving the dictionary’s contribution entangled with the selector’s. The SVD comparator gave no estimate.

title: Selective Language Damage with Parameter-Decomposition Subcomponents
text:
5 Limits of these conclusions
The result covers six edits in one four-layer model, three language pairs and two values of τ. The measured outcomes are protected-language CE on parliamentary text and English CE guards and KL. The confirmatory readout tests fixed edits on new text in the same languages; uncertainty varies session dates only (Section 2.5). Testing the selection rule in other models, explaining the edits’ selectivity and evaluating tasks beyond next-token prediction remain open.

title: Selective Language Damage with Parameter-Decomposition Subcomponents
text:
6 Conclusion
In this model, one subcomponent per target language, chosen from target and English text and calibrated to raise target CE by 0.5 or 1 nat/token on validation text, raised the CE of the related language by at most 0.0053 nat/token on 58 new session dates. Rank-one LoRA and full-matrix fine-tuning updates calibrated to the same validation rise raised it by about 0.03 to 0.41, and neuron edits by 0.42 to 0.88. All 18 simultaneous intervals of the differences lie below zero. A post hoc check found agreement in achieved target effects within ±0.1 nat/token in 15 of the 18 comparisons. In the other three the subcomponent edit’s target effect was larger on average, though one interval also allows a smaller effect. The advantage does not extend to English, where the learned updates move the output distribution less.
Exploratory comparisons on the development dates found the same direction against a whitened rank-one selector and against learned updates trained for 2,000 steps. The randomized-dictionary control found no edit to compare, and the selection history was not blind (Section 2.4). Together, the comparisons show that selective single-subcomponent edits exist for these three pairs in this model, with effects reproduced on a fixed confirmatory readout.
AI assistance. I used OpenAI Codex and Anthropic Claude for research planning, code development, data analysis, and manuscript preparation. Scientific Agent Skills (Kassis et al. 2026) supplied the scientific-writing, scientific-critical-thinking, peer-review and citation-management workflows used to review organization, claims and references.

text:
7 Method details

Subcomponents and text. The decomposition has 512 subcomponents each for query and key, 1,024 each for value and output, 3,072 for the MLP input and 3,584 for the MLP output matrix of each layer. The Europarl text comes from release v7 of the corpus (Koehn 2005), downloaded from https://www.statmt.org/europarl/v7/europarl.tgz. Each Europarl split has one 257-token window per session date (256 predictions). Each target has three draws of 64 of its 128 Europarl training windows. Calibration uses 32 target-language Europarl validation windows per target. The English validation set has 64 windows: 32 Europarl and 32 English-filtered Pile windows. The English retain pool has 256 windows: 128 of Europarl English training text, 64 of WikiText-2 validation text and 64 of English-filtered Pile validation text.
Selection. For softmax cross-entropy, the Fisher information matrix equals the generalized Gauss–Newton matrix (Martens 2020, sec. 9.2). It differs from the empirical Fisher, which uses the data’s labels (Kunstner et al. 2019, sec. 1). The curvature \(q_c\) is the mean squared directional score over the retain pool, with eight sets of labels sampled from \(W_0\) per window. The floor \(\varepsilon\) is the 1st percentile of \(q_c / \lVert
A_c\rVert^2\) over subcomponents. The top 64 subcomponents are re-ranked with the larger of \(q_c\) and a second estimate on 256 other English windows. The search raises the dose on the grid \(0.0625 \cdot \sqrt{2}^{\,k}\) for \(k = 0, \ldots, 10\), that is up to 2. Before any selection, \(q\) was checked against finite-difference curvature on English windows. The check, including contraction, batch splitting and scaling, passed on the NVIDIA L40S used for the original runs. On the tested A10 and L4, the batch-splitting test failed identically in the original and released implementations. The checked selection reruns are limited to the L40S, for the German target’s first draw with the VPD dictionary and one randomized dictionary. Fisher-label sampling depends on the GPU model, so selections can differ on other GPUs.
Calibration. The dose grid is scanned and the first crossing of τ is bracketed. Linear bisection, at most five steps, stops at the first point within the matching tolerance. The neuron edit scales the output weights of the top \(k\) neurons by \(1 - f\). Its calibration takes the smallest \(k\) among powers of two from 1 to 256 whose full removal reaches τ, then calibrates \(f\). The chosen \(k\) ranges from 2 to 256. The randomized-dictionary permutations use a separate seed per draw.
Learned updates. The objective is a hinge on target CE, \(\max(0, 1 - \Delta\mathrm{CE})\) per window, plus the KL divergence from \(W_0\) on the English retain pool with weight 1. Training uses Adam (Kingma and Ba 2015) with 10 warm-up steps and gradient clipping at 1.0, 8 target and 8 English windows per step, for 200 steps. The edit is the final update \(D\) scaled down, \(\beta D\) with \(\beta \le 1\), and \(\beta\) is calibrated like a dose. The learning rate was chosen once per target, on draw 0, by the lowest English validation KL at τ = 1. The LoRA grid was {1e-4, 3e-4, 1e-3, 3e-3} and the full-matrix fine-tuning grid {1e-6, 3e-6, 1e-5}. The choice was 3e-3 for LoRA and 1e-6 for full-matrix fine-tuning on all three targets, the top and the bottom of their grids.

7.1 Extended comparisons
The comparisons were specified before these runs. I measured the six subcomponent edits again, next to four comparators calibrated to the same τ:

SVD components. The selection rule of Section 2.1 is applied unchanged to the rank-one terms of a singular value decomposition of the 24 weight matrices. These terms reconstruct the weights, whereas VPD leaves a residual that is unchanged by its subcomponent edits.
A whitened rank-one selector. In each matrix, this procedure finds a direction outside the VPD dictionary with the largest squared target gradient relative to the damped K-FAC curvature of the English retain text (Martens and Grosse 2015), using the norm of that target–draw combination’s VPD subcomponent and the selector’s ε. It then scores the direction with the same rule and tests doses from 1/64 to 8.
Longer-trained rank-one LoRA and full-matrix fine-tuning. The learned updates are trained for 2,000 steps instead of 200, with a hinge margin of 1.5 instead of 1, wider learning-rate grids and three seeds per draw.

Each side of a contrast is the mean over its matched and usable runs. The analysis compares these means without pairing runs by draw. The contrasts form one simultaneous family. The learned-update contrasts are repeated as a second family without the runs flagged as unstable, 7 of the 27 LoRA runs. For each interval, the analysis reports its direction and whether it lies wholly within ±0.02 nat/token. These runs used a different GPU model, which changes the sampled Fisher labels. Selection found the same subcomponents in all nine target–draw combinations, and the subcomponent-edit readout matched the main readout within 1.5·10⁻⁶ nat/token.

Chronology of the exploratory comparisons. The comparisons, labels and limits were declared on 12 October 2026, before the runs. The 5% tolerance for reproducing the main selection’s curvature floor across GPU models was added after one selection had finished but before its result was read. The analysis rules were fixed before any readout, after the selection outcomes, learning-rate choices and target and English validation effects of the rate grid had been seen. The records were then frozen, and the readout was run. The analyzer’s two properties were implemented after readout but before any readout measurements were opened or analysed. This sequence comes from the author’s records and is not independently timestamped.
Diagnostics for the exploratory comparisons. A learned run is flagged as unstable if its English validation KL at step 2,000 is more than twice its minimum from step 100 onward. The second comparison family excludes these runs. A change of less than 10% in English validation KL between steps 1,500 and 2,000 is called a plateau. Only 6 of the 54 training runs used in the comparisons met it. Including the 18 additional learning-rate candidates gives 7 of 72, all full-matrix fine-tuning runs. This diagnostic does not establish convergence of the training objective and does not determine which edit is selected. At 200 steps the learned comparators’ learning rates lay at the edges of the tested grids. At 2,000 steps they still caused more related-language damage.


7.2 Readouts and intervals
Readouts. The development guards are Europarl English test text (64 windows), WikiText-2 test text (32 windows) and Pile test documents (512 windows). The confirmatory guard is English text from the 58 confirmatory dates. The confirmatory set has 48 main and 10 reserve dates, analysed as one set.
Intervals. Dates are resampled with replacement, one resample shared by every contrast of a family. Each contrast’s standard error is the standard deviation of its resampled means, and the interval is the estimate ± \(c\) standard errors. The critical value \(c\) is the 95% quantile, over resamples, of the largest absolute standardized deviation in the family. With 2,000 resamples (seed 0), \(c\) = 2.780 for the claim family on the 58 confirmatory dates and 2.814 on the 64 development dates. For the alternative subcomponent-selection family, \(c\) is 2.817 on the confirmatory dates and 2.772 on development.
Verdicts. The first applicable rule in the verdict table determines the result. No interval or a technical failure gives “not established”. A target flag in any used draw gives “effect not maintained”. An interval that excludes zero with the development sign gives “reproduced on confirm”, and with the opposite sign “not reproduced”. Anything else is “not established”.
Target gaps. The post hoc target gaps, the protected-CE contrasts and the corresponding protected-KL contrasts form one family of 54 coordinates per readout, with the per-date values averaged over draws. The family has a joint bootstrap over dates (20,000 resamples, seed 20261011) and a max-|t| critical value of 3.149 on the confirmatory readout and 3.158 on the development dates.


7.3 Protocol records and prior access

Freeze and readout. The selection rule, comparators, calibration, guard rule and analysis were fixed in code and a protocol, with a freeze record dated 11 October 2026. The development readout and its analysis ran right after the freeze. A second set of 58 session dates was read once, later the same day, with the frozen edits unchanged. An amendment written before any window was parsed fixed the readout procedure.
Prior knowledge. The research before the freeze was not blind. The German subcomponent 0.attn.o:268 had been chosen in an earlier experiment with Dutch in view, and it was the top German candidate in an earlier pilot run of this selector. Dutch, Portuguese and Italian text from the development splits, and the NTREX Dutch and Italian sets (Federmann et al. 2022), had been read or used in earlier development. The protected-language damage on the 64 development dates is therefore part of the development readout.
Pretraining. The Pile contains a European Parliament component (Gao et al. 2020, sec. 2.17). I did not establish whether the subset on which the model was trained includes it, so the dates are new to this workflow but may have appeared in pretraining.
Dates and hashes. The dates come from the documents’ own records and the project’s run log, and neither is independently timestamped. The original protocol, freeze record and frozen code list are not published. Their recorded hashes identify the files’ contents; the date of those contents remains unverified, so the records lack a timestamped preregistration.

Each alternative selection rule chooses one subcomponent, which is calibrated in the same way as the main edit:

Bushnaq ranks subcomponents the same way but trains the top 16, and his single-subcomponent edit used a subcomponent chosen by its label instead of the ranking (Bushnaq 2026). historical_atom uses the previously chosen subcomponent 0.attn.o:268 on the removal side, for German only. This reuses a previously chosen intervention with its selection fixed by the earlier experiment.

title: Transferring Learned Repairs Between Fine-Tunes
text:
1 Introduction
Fine-tuning can damage behaviour outside the intended task. Repeating the same recipe on new samples can reproduce that damage, so a repair learned for an earlier fine-tune may help repair the next one. The earlier fine-tune is the donor and its repair is the donor repair. We can keep the donor repair’s directions fixed and fit new scalar coefficients, or use it to initialize a repair whose directions can change.
The fine-tuning procedure deliberately worsens German next-token prediction and, as a side effect, raises Dutch cross-entropy (CE), a measure of prediction loss. This provides a controlled test: the repair must restore Dutch prediction quality while preserving the intended German change. I train the donor and two target fine-tunes independently from the same base model, using the same recipe on different samples from the same Europarl data distribution. The donor repair has one rank-one update per weight matrix. The primary comparison asks how much Dutch damage is recovered by rescaling its fixed directions and by allowing those directions to change. The descriptive secondary comparisons ask how donor initialization performs against fresh and random starts at each fit budget and step cap, and what it saves (Table 1).
I fit rank-one repairs with a KL objective on the model used in Goodfire’s adVersarial Parameter Decomposition (VPD) study (Bushnaq et al. 2026). The repairs operate directly on its weight matrices, independently of the decomposition.
Several methods reuse a weight update with fixed or learned scales. Task arithmetic adds or subtracts a weight difference with a single scale (Ilharco et al. 2023). RESTA adds one separately obtained safety vector to fine-tunes in several domains, using a fixed global scale in its main experiments (Bhardwaj et al. 2024). SafeGene keeps a distilled safety adapter frozen and learns one scalar per selected layer, improving on a coefficient of 1 (Wang et al. 2026, sec. 3.5 and 4.4). Such reuse can also fail. EnchTable’s preprint Table II reports a medical fine-tune that RESTA leaves less safe than before (Wu et al. 2026). Other work uses a learned object to initialize new training. In SPoT, soft prompts learned on source tasks initialize the prompt of a target task (Vu et al. 2022). These studies do not compare the two uses of one transferred update on the same target at matched rank and cost. This study makes that comparison at matched rank and reports the costs of each family.

title: Transferring Learned Repairs Between Fine-Tunes
text:
2 Setup
Model and fine-tunes. The base model is Goodfire’s four-layer decoder-only model of 67M parameters, trained on a subset of the Pile (Bushnaq et al. 2026, sec. 3.1; Gao et al. 2020). Each fine-tune trains an additive update \(D\) to the 24 weight matrices of the attention and MLP blocks. Embeddings and norms stay frozen. A hinge term raises German CE, and a KL term keeps English, French, Spanish and Italian, the retain languages, close to the base model. The text is Europarl session text (Koehn 2005). The donor fine-tune and the two targets follow the same recipe with different seeds and training dates (method details). Dutch is held out of fine-tuning. On the readout dates the primary target’s Dutch damage is 0.187 nat/token [0.178, 0.196] and the replication target’s 0.189 [0.180, 0.198].
Repair. A repair adds \(E_m = b_m a_m^{\top}\) to each of the 24 matrices of the fine-tuned model, so it has rank one per matrix. The vector \(a_m\) is the input factor and \(b_m\) is the output factor. The repair minimizes KL divergence from two teacher models across three groups of text. The fine-tuned model is the teacher on German, to preserve the intended effect, and on the retain languages. The base model is the teacher on Dutch, to undo the damage. Each term uses \(D_{\mathrm{KL}}(p_{\text{teacher}}\,\|\,p_{\text{repair}})\), averaged over the group’s predicted positions. The loss sums the mean KL of the three groups with equal weights. The repair norm is capped at the fine-tune norm, \(\lVert E\rVert_F \le \lVert D\rVert_F\). Every family trains full-batch for 600 steps at four learning rates and keeps checkpoints as candidates for selection. Families initialized from the donor repair scale it down if needed to meet the norm cap (method details).
Recovery. Recovery is the share of the fine-tune’s Dutch damage that a repair \(X\) removes, \[r_{\text{nl}}(X) = 1 - \frac{\mathrm{CE}_{\text{nl}}(X) - \mathrm{CE}_{\text{nl}}(\text{base})}{\mathrm{CE}_{\text{nl}}(\text{fine-tuned}) - \mathrm{CE}_{\text{nl}}(\text{base})}.\] Differences in recovery are reported in percentage points (pp).
In the scalar-only family, each donor repair update stays fixed and the repair is \(E_m = c_m b_m a_m^{\top}\). Fitting the coefficients \(c_m\) trains 24 parameters. The other families train one or both factors, as listed in Table 1.

Varying the fit budget and the step cap separates a gain in final recovery from a gain in reaching it sooner. The output-only and fresh families have counterparts in low-rank adapters. The output factor of an adapter matters more than its input factor when the input factor is random and frozen (Zhu et al. 2024). Here, the output-only family’s frozen input vectors are the donor repair’s trained ones. Fresh fitting uses the zero-output initialization of such adapters (Hu et al. 2022). A second seed of fresh and of random initialization, at the full budget only, shows how far a result moves between initializations. The first fresh seed starts from the same input vectors used to initialize the donor repair, while the second uses an independent draw.
Budgets and step caps. Each target has nested fit budgets of 256, 512 and 2,048 unique predicted tokens with a 2:1:1 split of Dutch, German and retain text. These budgets count prediction positions, excluding the initial context token of each window. A separate selection and diagnostic pool contains 57,344 prediction positions, shared by all families. Checkpoints at steps ≤50, ≤100 and ≤200 of the same runs form step-capped cells, alongside the full 600-step runs. Each family therefore has a grid of 3 budgets × 4 step caps. The cost appendix gives the costs of selection and of the additional scalar optimization.
Selection and readout. For every family and cell, a fixed rule chooses one candidate on separate selection dates: among the candidates that keep the fine-tune’s German effect and move Dutch toward the base model, it prefers higher Dutch recovery, subject to a guard against raising the CE of the retain languages (method details). The chosen repairs are read out once on 92 session dates from the validation period, separate from the project’s earlier data windows (data details). The selected checkpoint can precede the cell’s step cap. All cells of a target share one bootstrap over readout dates (Efron 1979), so contrasts are paired. Intervals are 95% percentile intervals.
Additional scalar optimization. At the 2,048-token budget, two additional runs optimize the scalar coefficients to convergence on the exact full-batch fit loss from two starts. The selection rule then chooses among the 48 training checkpoints and these 2 converged candidates. Both kinds are eligible, including the ordinary training checkpoints (appendix).
Interpretation rules. The primary contrast compares donor initialization with the scalar-only search with full-batch optimization at 2,048 tokens and 600 steps. An advantage of more than 3 pp is established if its whole interval lies above 3 pp, excluded if the whole interval lies below 3 pp, and undecided otherwise. I interpret this contrast on a target only if its Dutch damage is clear (the lower end of the readout interval is at least 0.025 nat/token), both selected repairs satisfy the readout constraints in Table 6, and scalar optimization converged from both starts. All other contrasts are descriptive, without multiplicity correction. Their intervals determine whether the sign is positive, negative or undecided. Five contrasts, marked in Table 3, are also assessed for equivalence within a ±2 pp band. The protocol fixes both margins without a stated derivation.

title: Transferring Learned Repairs Between Fine-Tunes
text:
4 Limits of these conclusions
The experiment uses one donor, one recipe and one model, with each target analysed separately. The bootstrap quantifies variation across readout dates for those targets. Variation across fine-tunes, donors and recipes remains unmeasured. Second seeds were run at the full budget only, leaving short-run advantages unassessed against seed variation.
The scalar-only shortfall applies to the tested search and norm cap (optimization details). The mechanism and the contribution of the donor repair’s input vectors remain unresolved (control details). The cost projection uses the first fresh seed as its reference and depends on the tested grid (cost accounting).
The repair addresses collateral Dutch CE damage after a fine-tune that deliberately worsens German prediction. Safety alignment and transfer of a new skill remain outside the study’s scope.

title: Transferring Learned Repairs Between Fine-Tunes
text:
5 Conclusion
For this model and recipe, at the full fitting budget, training a donor-initialized repair recovered 11.3 pp [+10.0, +12.7] and 20.4 pp [+19.0, +21.7] more of the Dutch damage than the tested scalar-only search over the donor repair’s fixed directions, including its converged full-batch candidates. The gap was nearly as large at 256 and 512 tokens. Donor initialization helped most with little fitting data and few steps. At the full budget, its advantage over fresh fitting was positive but inside the ±2 pp equivalence band, and comparable to the difference between two fresh seeds. On the tested grid, its cheapest reaching cell used one eighth as many fit-token presentations as fresh fitting’s cheapest reaching cell. When cost was minimized in unique tokens instead, both families reached the reference with 256 fit tokens.

6 Method details

Model and fine-tunes. The base model has 66,931,200 parameters (residual width 768, MLP width 3,072). The 24 matrices are the query, key, value, output and two MLP matrices of each layer. Each fine-tune trains with Adam (Kingma and Ba 2015) at learning rate 3e-6 for 200 steps on a hinge term with a 1-nat margin, \(\max(0, 1 - \Delta\mathrm{CE}_{\text{de}})\) per window, and a KL term of weight 1 on the retain languages. Its checkpoint is chosen on German validation dates.
Repairs. Families initialized from the donor repair use \(\min(1, \lVert D\rVert_F / \lVert
E_{\text{donor}}\rVert_F)\, E_{\text{donor}}\). Fresh input factors have variance \(1/d_{\text{in}}\). Every family uses 10 warm-up steps, followed by a constant learning rate, with gradient clipping at 1.0. Saving a checkpoint every 50 steps at four learning rates (Table 5) gives 48 candidates.

The learning-rate grids stayed fixed for the 50-step runs. Several output-only cells and the donor-initialized replication cell at 512 tokens select the first checkpoint at the smallest learning rate. Repeated values across step caps can therefore arise from checkpoint reuse alone. Advantages over fresh and random initialization change nonmonotonically as the step cap or budget increases.
Random initialization compares initial directions at matched norm, with both factors subsequently trained. The current controls do not compare the donor’s trained input vectors with frozen random input vectors while training only the output factor.
Selection. A candidate is feasible if the ratio of German damage with and without the repair lies between 0.9 and 1.1, its German KL drift from the fine-tuned model is at most 0.05 times the base model’s German KL from the fine-tune, and it moves Dutch toward the base model. Feasible candidates are ranked by Dutch recovery, then by smaller norm. Of the top five, the first that raises no retain language’s CE by more than 0.01 nat/token is chosen.
Data. Portuguese, a seventh language, is measured as a diagnostic on the selection and readout dates. Its selection windows are included in the selection-token and evaluation costs. Its role is diagnostic only; it is excluded from the loss and selection constraints.
The data check would have excluded a readout date if a scan found it in the project’s data, pilot or run files, or if its text window duplicated text already in use. All dates passed. The scan covers recorded project use; prior model exposure to these texts remains unresolved. Selection uses 32 dates and readout uses 92 dates. Each date contributes one 257-token window (256 next-token predictions) from the same turn in every language. Both targets use the same 92 readout dates. The fit windows and selection dates are separate from the donor repair’s. The fit budgets are nested. At the 256-token budget, one Dutch window contributes 128 predictions, one German window 64, and four retain windows 16 each. The 512-token budget doubles these counts. At 2,048 tokens, four Dutch and two German windows contribute 256 predictions each, and one retain window contributes 128 per language.
Study record. According to my records, the rules, margins and families were fixed in a dated protocol before the readout data were built and the target fine-tunes were run. One author-dated amendment, made before any target fine-tune or readout, fixed the readout data and clarified the wording of the primary interpretation while keeping the decision rules unchanged. The protocol, amendment and project log remain unpublished and lack independent timestamps, so their chronology rests on the author’s records rather than verifiable preregistration.
Uncertainty. The joint bootstrap uses 5,000 date resamples shared across both blocks of a target. Each resample recomputes the mean damages and then takes their recovery ratios. The ratio is therefore formed at the aggregate level. The readout constraints are applied to the point estimates on all dates. Equivalence is assessed for the five contrasts marked in Table 3; equivalence between donor and random initialization remains unestablished at every budget and step cap.

text:
8 Cost accounting

With \(C^*\) a family’s cheapest reaching cost, found separately in each currency, reuse pays off for more than \[
K^* = \frac{C_{\text{donor}}}{C^*(\text{fresh}) - C^*(\text{donor initialization})}
\] targets (Table 4). In fit-token presentations, both cheapest cells use the shortest step cap in the grid, and donor initialization uses its smallest budget. The one-eighth ratio is therefore the budget ratio 2,048/256, set by the tested grid. With the donor repair’s cost of 3,686,400 presentations, this gives \(K^* \approx 10.3\). The calculation amortizes the measured per-target costs. The 11-target break-even is a cost projection; the experiment used two targets. The accounting exclusions are detailed below.
Every donor-initialized cell reaches the reference, down to 256 tokens and 50 steps. Fresh fitting reaches it with 2,048 tokens at every step cap, but with 256 or 512 tokens only at step caps of 200 to 600. No scalar-only cell reaches it, and neither does the fixed donor repair (Figure 3).
A random start saves no presentations on the primary target. On the replication target, it reaches the reference with fewer presentations than fresh fitting, \(K^* = 18\), charged with the full donor cost although it uses only the donor repair’s norm.
Unique tokens count a cell’s fit tokens plus the 57,344 predicted tokens on the selection dates (32 dates × 7 languages × 256). Fit-token presentations count the optimizer steps of all four learning rates up to the cap multiplied by the unique fit tokens. GPU seconds count training seconds prorated to the cap, plus the cell’s share of selection evaluation according to its number of candidates. For the scalar-only search with full-batch optimization, presentation and GPU-second costs include both additional optimization runs and the evaluation of 48 checkpoints used to choose the second start.
No cell includes the readouts of the base and fine-tuned models or the damage check before fitting. Presentations also exclude the forward passes used for selection. The donor repair’s one-time cost is 131,072 unique tokens (its 73,728 fit tokens and the selection tokens), 3,686,400 presentations (3 learning rates × 200 steps × 6,144 tokens per minibatch), and an estimated 336 GPU seconds for training, selection and readout. The donor fine-tune is excluded because, in use, the donor model already exists.
The reference’s paired interval against itself is [0, 0] by construction. At 256 fit tokens with a 600-step cap, fresh fitting reaches the reference narrowly: its interval’s lower end is −1.985 pp on the primary target and −1.957 pp on the replication target, against the −2 pp threshold. This cell sets the lowest unique-token cost for fresh fitting.
The break-even calculation uses the first fresh seed as its reference, with its size set by the tested grid (Section 3.3). Sensitivity to a different reference seed remains unevaluated.

title: Some Studies of Language Model Weight Edits
text:
Some Studies of Language Model Weight Edits
Changing a model's weights can affect more than the intended behaviour. These studies examine selective language edits and the reuse of repairs for collateral damage, using Goodfire's 67M-parameter model.




Selective language editing
This study tests how selectively weight edits can weaken one language while sparing a close relative, following up on Lucius Bushnaq’s exploration of fine-tuning with parameter decomposition. Across three related-language pairs, selected subcomponent edits caused less damage to the related language than learned updates and neuron edits calibrated to the same target effect on validation text. The learned updates preserved English predictions better.

Repair transfer
This study tests ways to reuse an earlier repair on two fine-tunes trained independently from the same base model on samples from the same data distribution. Using the repair as an initialization removed more Dutch damage than fresh fitting when data and steps were limited, while fresh fitting nearly caught up at the full budget. Rescaling the repair's fixed directions left more Dutch damage.

title: Repair transfer
section: The same starting repair, two ways to reuse it
text:
The same starting repair, two ways to reuse it
The earlier fine-tune is the donor and its correction is the donor repair. The two new fine-tunes use different Europarl session dates. Each repair adds a rank-one update to each of 24 weight matrices, with the model’s other weights fixed. Each update is formed from an input vector and an output vector. The repairs operate directly on the weight matrices, independently of Goodfire’s parameter decomposition.
I reuse the donor repair in two ways: keep its input and output vectors fixed and learn 24 scalar coefficients, or start from the donor repair and train both vectors. Fresh fitting learns both vectors from a new initialization. All three have the same rank, objective and norm limit, so the comparison asks what the earlier repair contributes.

title: Repair transfer
section: Keeping the directions leaves damage behind
text:
Keeping the directions leaves damage behind
Recovery is the fraction of the fine-tune’s extra Dutch prediction loss removed by a repair. At the full budget, fitting scalar coefficients only recovers about 87% of the Dutch damage on the first target and 78% on the second. Donor initialization, which lets the directions change, raises recovery to about 98–99%. Fresh initialization also works well. All full-budget repairs shown preserved the German effect and met the constraints on the other languages.
Fitting budgets exclude a separate selection and diagnostic pool of 57,344 prediction positions, shared by all families.

section: The donor helps most when fitting is constrained
text:
The donor helps most when fitting is constrained
Fresh fitting also recovers most of the damage, so I compare how much the donor start helps at different fitting budgets. At the full budget, donor initialization leads the first fresh seed by 1.1–1.4 percentage points. Both confidence intervals lie inside the study’s ±2 percentage-point equivalence band, and the lead is comparable to differences between two fresh seeds. At 256 fit tokens and 50 steps, the lead is about 4 percentage points; only one fresh seed was tested at that budget.

title: Selective language editing
text:
Edit one rank-one subcomponent
Goodfire’s adVersarial Parameter Decomposition (VPD) writes a weight matrix as a sum of rank-one subcomponents plus a residual. Each subcomponent is formed from an input vector and an output vector. The edit changes one selected subcomponent’s scalar coefficient, keeping both vectors fixed. All other coefficients and the residual stay fixed. A coefficient of zero removes the selected contribution. A negative coefficient reverses it.

Rank-one LoRA learns both vectors of an update to the same matrix. Full-matrix fine-tuning can change all 24 weight matrices, and neuron edits scale selected neurons’ output weights.
I measure next-token prediction on parliamentary text. The selection and training procedures use target and English text. The selection rule ranks subcomponents by their estimated effect on the target language relative to their effect on English. Each method’s edit is calibrated to raise the target language’s prediction error, measured as cross-entropy (CE), by the same amount on validation text: 0.5 or 1 nat per token. A nat is a unit of information based on natural logarithms. 1 nat is about 1.44 bits. A larger rise means worse next-token prediction. Matching this rise gives the methods the same intended effect before I compare their side effects on separate evaluation text.

Across all three pairs and both calibrated effects, related-language CE rose by about 0.0003–0.0053 nat/token. The subcomponent edits caused less related-language damage than each comparator: all 18 simultaneous intervals for those differences lie below zero. These comparisons share the same six fixed edits.
Earlier development had used related-language text and identified the German subcomponent. The new dates test the fixed edits; the selection history was not blind.
The methods differ in what they preserve. The subcomponent edits cause less damage to the related language, while the learned updates keep English predictions closer to the original model, measured by KL divergence.

title: Selective language editing
text:
Longer training and alternative directions
To check how the comparison depends on the training recipe, I trained the learned updates for 2,000 steps under an expanded recipe. These updates generally reduced related-language damage, but still caused more than the subcomponent edits. A separate selector searched for rank-one directions outside VPD’s fixed set of subcomponents. Its edits also caused more related-language damage; it reused the selected subcomponent’s norm.
A randomized-dictionary control produced no comparable edit, so the dictionary’s contribution remains unresolved.
These exploratory comparisons reuse development text examined earlier. Convergence of the learned updates was not established. The paper gives the comparison details and study limits.
